newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Irish paper on gas liberalisation wins praise.
newsitem.headline: Irish paper on gas liberalisation wins praise.

text.p: European Union diplomats expressed cautious optimism on Wednesday that agreement could be reached on liberalising natural gas markets following this week's first discussions on a new proposal from the Irish presidency.
But they stressed that the negotiations were still at an early stage and success could not be guaranteed.
"In general terms, I think (member states') delegations were rather positive," said one EU diplomat about the talks on Monday and Tuesday on the new presidency paper.

The differences between the member states were not as fundamental as they were in the negotiations on opening up EU electricity markets. "I think this is after all going to be easier," the diplomat added.
The Council's energy working group will meet again on Monday to continue discussions on the text. So far, member states' energy officials have gone through about half of the articles.
"We feel that we've made progress," an Irish official said, adding that "it is obviously not going to be easy."

The talks have not yet touched upon several of the potentially controversial items in the dossier, including the level of market opening, the issue of eligible customers and the long-term "take or pay" contracts, which currently dominate the highly concentrated European gas industry.
"All the controversial stuff we've not come to yet," one diplomat said.
Unlike the agreement on electricity, which foresees a gradual and progressive opening up of national markets, the presidency paper on gas liberalisation proposes a one-off liberalisation only.

It uses the same method to calculate the share of the market that would be open to competition as the deal on electricity, including a threshold to determine which consumers will be allowed to shop around freely for the best deal.
This may be one of the most controversial elements of the dossier, but diplomats were reluctant to comment as long as no concrete figures had been put on the table.
"I think personally it depends on the level (of market opening) you choose from the beginning," one EU diplomat said.
The natural gas dossier will dominate the EU's energy policy work during the final months of the year, even if no one expects an agreement before 1997, possibly during the Dutch presidency.
EU energy ministers will discuss the dossier at their meeting on December 3.
The presidency paper takes the place of the amended Commission proposal COM(93)643, which was put forward in 1993 but left in abeyance while the EU focused on the twin directives on electricity.
The 1993 proposal said the liberalisation of the gas markets should be implemented in phases "in order to enable industry to adjust in a flexible and ordered manner to its new environment."
Diplomats hope some aspects of the electricity deal, which foresees a gradual and limited liberalisation, can be used for natural gas, removing some potential obstacles.
Under the deal on electricity nearly a quarter of the EU's market will be open to competition from January 1999 at the earliest. This would rise to about a third by 2003.
It was the result of a compromise, mainly between Germany, which pushed for wide liberalisation, and France, wary of any dramatic opening up of markets.
Officials hope for more flexibility in the gas talks, even if the positions of some countries are not yet clear.

Britain and the Netherlands, both big producers, would like to see rapid and far-reaching liberalisation while other member states take a more cautious line, stressing the need to guarantee the security of supply.
